newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU PUSHES ON WITH MEDIA LAW.
newsitem.headline: EU PUSHES ON WITH MEDIA LAW.

text.p: European publishers were up in arms on Tuesday as the European Commission prepared to push on with plans for EU legislation to curb domination of the media by a handful of media moguls.

Ahead of a meeting of the EU executive in Strasbourg on Wednesday a majority of the 20 Commissioners had come round to the idea of an EU directive to protect media pluralism and were expected to agree to the plan in principle, EU officials said.
Further discussions on the details of the plan would be necessary, however, a Commission spokeswoman said.
"We think that another discussion would be helpful," she said.

The Commission plan is a response to strong demands from the European Parliament for EU legislation to protect pluralism and democracy in the world of media moguls like Silvio Berlusconi and Rupert Murdoch.

European publishers, on the other hand, arguing the legislation will hinder their ability to adapt and compete in a fast changing media world, have carried out a frenzied lobbying effort against the plan.

"We have explained why we don't believe a media pluralism directive will benefit Europe's media companies and can only conclude that they don't want to hear the truth," Sir Frank Rogers, chairman of the European Publishers' Council, said in a statement on Tuesday.
"We have been startled by the Commission's unwillingness to listen to the very companies that their proposals will affect."
A draft Commission document made available to Reuters says that domination should be judged in terms of audience share rather than number of outlets or control held by a company.
Under the approach adopted by the Commission companies would not be able to extend their control of a country's television and radio stations once their audience share reaches a certain level.

The ceiling has been set at 30 percent for owners operating in only one field, whether it be television or radio, and an average of 10 percent per medium for those operating in several areas, including the written press.

The Commission, seeking to play down its attack on the media moguls, says the legislation is necessary to prevent different rules on media pluralism from one country to another damaging the EU's single market.

The European Newspapers Publishers' Association said in a recent statement that the development of the information society required press companies in Europe, whatever their size and location, to be able to become truly multimedia companies and to invest in cross-media ventures.
